idiom_name: generic closure { $0 } / func identity<T>(_ x: T) -> T { x }
implementation_notes: Swift ships no global identity function — the id(_:) symbol in Apple's docs is SwiftUI's view-identity modifier, not a value-level id like Haskell's — so the realization is a one-line generic function 'func identity<T>(_ x: T) -> T { x }' or, inline, the shorthand closure '{ $0 }', which fully replaces the classic helper-object structure. It slots into the stdlib's fold: reduce(_:_:) takes an explicit initialResult (the monoid's identity VALUE, e.g. 0 for +, [] for concatenation), while the identity FUNCTION serves as the base of function composition — reducing an array of transforms with identity yields an empty pipeline that passes input through. For key-extraction APIs, the key path '\.self' is Swift's type-safe spelling of 'derive no key'. A concrete identity<T> specialization is statically dispatched and the optimizer inlines it away; the classic form stays justified when you define custom composition operators (>>>), where identity is the neutral element of the (T) -> T endomorphism monoid.
pitfalls: Function values have no stable identity in Swift: '==' and '===' do not exist on closures (the optimizer may merge, thunk or reabstract them freely), so you cannot test transform == identity to detect the no-op case — guard with an enum/flag instead.

Passing a function through generic contexts forces reabstraction thunks (SR-7179 shows repeated identity wrapping overflowing the stack in unoptimized builds); storing identity as an '(T) -> T' value in a hot loop can allocate where the inlined specialization would not.

In a Void/discarding slot, '{ $0 }' silently does nothing while still satisfying the signature — a forgotten real transform compiles without warning, so tag pipeline steps for debugging rather than relying on output inspection.
Do not name it 'id': that collides with SwiftUI's .id(_:) modifier and Objective-C bridging conventions — the canonical Swift spellings are 'identity' or the inline closure '{ $0 }'.
